p: Thank you. Is the Administration open to securing more funding to expand CPI even further?

Thank you for the question. We have, since the fall of 2021, 425 million dollars in baseline mayoral capital funding for continuing the program beginning then. We've then, therefore, got 50 million dollars annually to complete renovations in 10 sites per year

for the next 10 years, and very much look forward to continuing that work.

I just want to go back to something you mentioned in your testimony, and pardon me if I misheard. Did you say that 0.8 percent out of the 85 percent goal, represents 63 people without close access to parks? Is that what you said?
63,000. Okay. I'm like, okay, 63, that's not bad. Thank you. And, is that in a particular neighborhood, or is that just across the city?
That's across the city.

Thank you. Is the idea of funding Parks through property tax revenue, a tax increment finance district, or special park district, as is done in other cities such as Chicago, a viable one for New York City? Is that solution viable for New York City?

Thanks for the question, Chair.

You know, I think Parks Department is always open to… there's been a lot of interest and excitement about, you know, the needs of parks in the city, and, you know, we're delighted to take part in those conversations. Speaking to the specific funding models of that sort, you know, it's a conversation we're happy to take part in. I don't think we're prepared at this time to kind of opine, and obviously we want to do that in consultation with, you know, OMB and a lot of other, you know, Mayor's Office stakeholders, but we're very intrigued and interested in a lot of the creative approaches that have been taking place across the country, and I think we think there's a lot to learn.
Has Parks actually considered it, or it hasn't really been top of mind?

I'm not aware that that funding model could be implemented by the agency, like, at its own discretion. I believe that would require, you know, I think there are other regulatory and policy steps that would need to be put into place, so I wouldn't say we have contemplated it, because I don't, you know, if it were to happen, it would have to require a series of more complicated

discussions and policy decisions, so I can't say that we've, you know, planned, but we're aware of the interest in both that funding model and others, and it's something we're watching very closely.
Okay. That's good to know. Are any other conservancies being planned for the near future that would run and maintain any of DPR's parks?

Yeah. Thanks for the question. We're very proud of our partnership with organizations, some of which range in size, you know, from small, sort of informal, what we call friends of parks groups, civic associations all over the city, to larger, you know, conservancies, formal conservancies that have license agreements with the City, and today I'm not aware of any sort of new conservancies that are coming online, so to speak, but we definitely are in a series of conversations with groups that are growing in capacity, that are very interested in playing a formalized role, and there's a lot of different ways to go about those structures, and we want to make sure that it will

serve the park best, and obviously, you know, in terms of the, each group is different, has different capacity, different interests, each park is different, that's, you know, that may be assisted by such a group, so those conversations, there are, you know, dozens, if not more, of groups that are, you know, out there growing and providing great value, and, you know, and we're in discussions about formalizing, you know, several of those agreements in a variety of fashions, but nothing to announce today that we would say is kind of coming online.
Okay. I guess as a follow-up to that, does Parks encourage such organizing?

We certainly encourage New Yorkers to get involved in their parks, and that can happen in a variety of ways, from informal, you know, volunteer groups to, you know, frankly, just park visitors, you know, cleaning up after themselves, right? There's a lot of different ways that people can support their local park. There are great organizations that have grown over time and are doing incredible work in our parks, and, you know, we very much value those partnerships, for sure.
But particularly friends groups and conservancies, does Parks encourage the formation of those type of organizations?

We do. We don't see it as a necessity, but it is an incredible engagement tool to make sure that, you know, New Yorkers are interested in their parks, and we found it's very helpful. It's nice to have an entity to kind of point them to, right? Something that has some structure around it. We do find that we don't think it's a necessity by any means. There are incredible parks in our system, that don't have a formalized group attached to it, and that's fine as well.
Is it helpful in terms of maintenance?
It can be. It certainly can be, but, you know, we're obviously dedicated to keeping our parks clean in the best condition possible, regardless of whether there's a group or not.

Thank you.

What efforts has DPR engaged in to determine which areas of the city are in the most need of green space?

Thank you for that question, Chair. As we mentioned in our testimony, we're proud to be the agency tasked with planning and managing and growing our green space, and we do that by carefully assessing where there is need across the city. As I mentioned, in 2015, the City began with, under the One NYC, a strategy to identify how we could reduce the number of New Yorkers that were not within a walking distance to parks. Again, that goal of achieving 85 percent of New Yorkers that are within a walking distance to parks by 2030 was really the driver to be able to assess whether we're, what state we're in now, and how we achieve that goal. We look citywide at the data on open space. We look at the open space across not just our property, but other entities as well, and with that, we're able to assess where the gaps are, and it's really that approach that's allowed us to identify where there are needs. So, in addition to this Walk to Park initiative, we have also zeroed in on a strategy to

try to ensure that we are poised to be able to then implement additional open space to take advantage of opportunities as they arise. So, that's our community-based ULURP initiative, our neighborhood ULURP program, and through that program, we identified 19 community districts across the city that had both large populations above a certain threshold, open space needs, ratios below a certain threshold, and/or a percent poverty that indicated need for investment. And with that program, that's one of the main ways in which we are assessing where there's need for green space, and how we can actually get to closing those gaps.
And have you published the data from your findings?

We currently have succeeded in going through ULURP for two of the community districts, and so that was a public process through which we go through ULURP, and I think we've shared all of that information with each of the districts as we go through that process. And we're now steadily working towards the rest of the community districts, and are currently focusing on Queens Community District too.

I just want to take a moment to acknowledge the presence of Council Member Salaam, P. Sanchez, and Council Member Krishnan. What areas of the city does DPR see as being in the most need of open and green space?

Thank you for the question, Chair. We have priority community districts that meet this criteria of really being in most need of closing these Walk to Park gaps. In the Bronx, Community Districts 9, 11, and 12. In Brooklyn, 5, 7, 11, 12, 14, 15, and 17.
I'm sorry, can you just, just a little slow.
Very happy to share this information with you, obviously, after the hearing. Brooklyn is 5, 7, 11, 12, 14, 15, and 17.
By chance, do you know what those neighborhoods are?

They span quite a bit. I know Marine Park is, I believe,

one of them in that district, but we can certainly get you a map and show you those neighborhoods.
I'd appreciate that. Thank you.
Queens has Districts 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 9, and 12, and Staten Island is District 1.

Okay. We have some work to do. Aside from developing or renovating parks and playgrounds, or planting trees, what are some of the other efforts DPR has engaged in over the years to help bring green space to neighborhoods that are in need?

Thank you for that question. Yes. In addition to the Walk to Park program and the neighborhood ULURP program, we look for opportunities to partner with other organizations and agencies to provide access to parks and open spaces whenever we can. One of our most successful programs has been the Schoolyard to Playground collaboration with both non-agency partners and with, of course, the public schools. We've also worked in

rezonings with our partners at the Department of City Planning to make sure that we're able to take opportunities to identify any new needs that come and be able to plan for the access needed for future New Yorkers, and work with privately operated public space owners when that's appropriate as well. We're also always in the process of making sure that the open spaces that we do have are well programmed, making them even more accessible and inviting, and in natural areas in particular, for example, we've really focused on stewardship and providing at hundreds of events every year to get people out to their open spaces, and with that we've been able to engage, you know, thousands of volunteers per year.

Thank you. Final question, final two questions from me, and then I'll turn it over to my Colleagues. The Council passed a slightly related bill in 2022, Local Law 10 of 2023, which required DPR with other appropriate agencies to review City-owned sites on streets with dead-end and land that abuts highway entrances, underpasses, and exits that the land that is suitable for the planting of

trees or other vegetation or creating green spaces. The report required from that bill was due in 2024 but has still not been submitted. Can you share an update on when that will be completed?
Yeah. We want to thank you, Council Member, for bringing this to our…
Council Member Krishnan's bill.

Yes. Very much so. Thanks for bringing this to our attention. Yeah. The Local Law did require that an agency or office designated by the Mayor would consult with all the, you know, the various entities that you mentioned, DEP, DOT, DCAS, including Parks, to undertake this site review. We're actually not able to speak to the status. I'm not aware that an entity was indeed designated by the previous Administration so we're going to need to sort of, but our colleagues are aware of the status of this, so, you know, we appreciate this having been brought to our attention and we'll try to get you an update as soon as we can.

I'd appreciate that. Thank you.

With that, I'm going to turn it over to Council Member Wong.

Okay. Thank you, Chair. I'm reading the statement here from the Parks Department, and it says that we look forward to work closely with DOT as they kick off their Cool Pavement pilot later this year, but we do not believe that a parallel park-specific pilot should be implemented at this time until the results of the DOT pilot can be comprehensively assessed. Now, I understand that DOT is also doing this, but Parks covers different spaces. Why are we waiting for DOT's program when Parks can start identifying parks and playgrounds that are heat islands, very specifically playgrounds, you know, and work to reduce that? It gives away responsibility or it kicks the can down the road for another Commissioner to deal with. Can you respond to that?

Yeah, absolutely. Thank you, Council Member. And again, to be very clear, Parks is doing a lot of work to reduce heat island effect in a variety of different ways that we also mentioned in

our testimony, including greening spaces that were within our, you know, and including using lighter colored tiles for our safety surface. We're very mindful of that. This specific technical exercise, the cool pavement piece, you know, DOT, we're working very closely with them. They are looking at spaces, incorporating spaces that we believe are actually commensurate or quite comparable to what we would consider park-type spaces, plazas, pedestrian areas, what have you, and we think there's going to be a lot to learn from those efforts. So, we're very dedicated to reducing heat island effect in all of our, you know, through greening, through planting. Those efforts will continue and on a parallel path as the City undergoes this pilot as required by last year's law, you know, we think there's going to be a lot of, you know, great lessons to learn. We're already working closely with DOT. They're aware of the interest in making sure that there are, you know, comparable lessons that can be sort of gleaned from their exercise. We'll be involved and we're looking very closely at that exercise.
Yeah. What I'm saying is that this bill 805 targets playgrounds and land under the jurisdiction of the
Yes.
That's not DOT's jurisdiction.

Correct. However, we would suggest that undertaking two separate pilots to achieve a similar goal is not the sort of coordination and thoughtful use of resources that, you know, that the City deserves. So, we believe that there's a lot to be learned from the pilot that's already required by law. There will be space… our understanding is DOT is still going through their site selections, but we believe there will be sites that are chosen that will be… that will provide helpful intelligence for us to learn from and to adopt and to pursue on our own merits, and we look forward to kind of learning from that.
How much time do I have? I still have time. Okay. Yeah.

No, I just want to be clear. Does the Parks Department have the goal of reducing dangerous heat that children may be

subjected to while spending time in parks and playgrounds?
Yes. Very much, and as we described in our testimony, there's a variety of efforts that the agency undertakes to address that very concern.
Then is the Parks Department supportive of projects that reduce dangerous heat children may be subject to while spending time in parks and playgrounds?
We are, and we implement them constantly.
But then what is the issue with the bill here that you seem that…

The issue is that the City is going to be undergoing a cool pavement pilot in coordination, led by DOT, but in coordination with multiple agencies. We believe that parallel pilots as a general like management strategy isn't advisable.
All right. Then did the Parks Department recommend changes? Why did the Parks Department recommend changes that almost completely erase the bill that reduces the heat in parks and playgrounds?

In coordination, first of all, this is a dialogue that's happening with our partners at DOT, with the Law Department, with the Mayor's Office, and we believe, and we're happy to discuss this with you and your team, we believe that you know for the bill to advance, we'd be interested in seeing incorporating more language to work with the law that's been enacted as opposed to creating a wholly separate and parallel process.
All right. I looked at the edits. The changes that the Administration recommended gives me the impression that you do not want to improve the well-being of the children.
Well, I can assure you, sir, that's incorrect. We very much care about the well-being and safety of all New Yorkers, including our children.

All right. Well, recommendations to help this City implement a program that makes it a safer and more comfortable place are welcome. Shirking responsibility is not welcome, and then I feel that after reading your edits.

Well, we're sorry you feel that way. We'd like to continue in the

conversation, as I think our testimony made clear. This agency is not shirking any responsibility, but we do want to move forward in exploring new avenues in a thoughtful and efficient manner.
Okay. Thank you. Thank you, Chair.
Thank you, Council Member. I'm going to turn it over to Council Member Narcisse.

Thank you, Chair, and thank you for being here. I love Parks, so I wish we can bring the money up, but my question is going to be around the dogs around our park. Does the Department track dog waste complaints separately from general park cleanliness complaints, and if so, what does that data show over the last three to five years, and how many 3-1-1 calls or complaints have been submitted specifically related to dog waste in the parks, and is the number trending up or down? How many fines have been issued to dog owners for failure to clean up waste in the parks annually? You know I love parks, so that's the reason I'm asking this.

No. It's a great question, and we appreciate it, Council Member. You know, I think there's been a lot of dialogue about the challenges. You know, there's a lot of press coverage and a lot of community dialogue about dog waste problems all over the city, including, you know, sidewalks and our partners at Sanitation. You know, we want to really strongly encourage all New Yorkers, you know, we all love our pets, our dogs, but we do need to be cleaning up after them properly, so we encourage all New Yorkers, obviously, to do that. You mentioned, so I'll clarify that dog waste is very much a data point that is included in our comprehensive parks inspection program. So, to be clear, this is a rigorous, comprehensive, deep dive, if you will, inspection of parks that's taken randomly, and it is conducted separately from our maintenance and operations team. So, it's similar to what you might, if you ever worked in retail, they have secret shopper sort of campaigns, so it's similar in that. They're independent visits, and they're very, very detailed, and dog waste is very much a data point that can lead to, you know, the

passing or failure of a given inspection. So, we can… I don't have those data points on hand at the moment, but we can certainly provide historical data about dog waste as a data point in parks in your District or wherever. Similarly, we can get you information about the summons that are issued by our Parks Enforcement Patrol officers. That's something, you know, whether it's dogs off leash or dog waste concerns, that's something we can definitely, you know, we should be able to get you data on that, and I think if I'm…
So, you don't have the data for me? Okay.
On dog waste? No, I don’t.
Because in a greenery, very beautiful park, you take your kids to run in the park and lay down, you don't want this to be a problem.

We agree 100 percent. You know, it's something we take very, very seriously. It can be obviously very detrimental to the experience of anyone who's ever closely encountered it on your shoes or what-have-you. It's very unpleasant,

obviously. It's something we take seriously, and we're happy to get you the more detailed data and metrics on that following this hearing.

All right. I have a few others, but I think we… The thing that I'm looking at the parks where we have 63,000, I believe, people not really having good access, and when I look at them, and especially in this Community Board 17 and District 58, we only have one little park, and it's concrete so I'm talking about the whole area. In Community Board 18, the same thing. I'm shocked to see that, you know, in South Side of Brooklyn, closer to the belt, all along we have parks, but in the middle, we don't have nothing going on. And what's the plan to improve in those areas in terms of green spaces? Do you have any plan for those areas? It's almost zero green space.

Thank you very much for the question, Council Member. We are continuing through primarily this program right now, our Neighborhood ULURP, to go systematically through the city, based on the data we have on open space, residents, and other indicators of percent poverty, to look at where there are gaps that are

priorities to fill. We certainly are very willing to look at other places and opportunities. You know, we've always been open to trying to opportunistically look for opportunities. Our Neighborhood ULURP program, however, will set us up in a community district to be able to take action when there are willing sellers, and when there are opportunities. So, between that and also looking at when there are rezonings, and when there are partnerships with our public schools, those are some of our primary tools to make sure that, in dense neighborhoods, we ensure that there's as much access to open space as possible.

Yeah. And now, probably a little off topic, we don't have no community centers. Coming to a park, we don't have no greenery. (TIMER CHIME) What's the plan to have community centers throughout our communities, and that's kind of like, you can build it with the greenery on top. So, Chair, I know you look at that. That's one of the problems, and that problem, I call it penny-wise, dollar-foolish, because when those kids don't have nothing to do, idle hands and idle mind, you know what the, is it devil's name, I don’t

really use it, but we need to be using preventive approach, not letting those kids to be trapped in the system that they should not be. So, if we have places like centers, are you promoting community centers like Shirley Chisholm? We only have one for so many decades, and y'all pride, some folks are proud to say, oh, we haven't had for so many years, but I think we're failing our youth, because that's where they supposed to be in the first place. Any plan in your life, because I know I'm talking about one, to be in where we have a lot of gun violence that happen. So, I feel like we should be focusing on those kind of inner green, like, how could I put it, you can use the rooftop for greenery, you can use the surrounding area, and I think that we should be focused on that. Any plan on that, when it comes to community centers?

Yeah. Thanks for the question, Council Member. And, you know, we love our recreation centers. They are a cornerstone of the facilities that offer incredible engagement and recreation and health opportunities, not just for our children, but, you know, adults, senior citizens. The membership

rates are free for anyone age 24 and younger. They're extremely affordable for senior citizens, persons with disabilities, military veterans, and even the base level is hundreds and hundreds and hundreds of dollars cheaper than your typical, you know, chain fitness club. So, we're very, very proud of our facilities. We're very excited to open to Shirley Chisholm. It's been a huge hit. The local community has been, you know, and we're happy we'll be opening up an additional three or four over the next couple years. Mary Cali Dalton in Staten Island, Soundview in the Bronx, and I'll note that, that effort, which, you know, which began several years ago, because it is a time-consuming and resource-intensive effort. These are state-of-the-art facilities that, you know, with construction in New York City, it won't be any surprise, can cost, you know, you know, 100, 150 million dollars. Like, these are major investments, but necessary investments. As you say, a preventative approach to engaging youth and, you know, saving at the end of the day, you know, possibly millions and millions and millions of dollars of health care, you know, the criminal justice system, like, you name it, like all those other impacts that can happen. We

believe that our centers are a vital and a wise investment. So, we're excited to be advancing the projects that are going to be coming online. We're always looking for more opportunities. I know you've been very keenly, you've been a vocal and energetic advocate for a center in your District. That's something we want to continue that conversation. It is a serious investment that requires, you know, the provision of a lot of resources, and that can be a complicated conversation, but it's one we're very, very, you know, excited to have.

I love complicated conversation. I'm a registered nurse and ER nurse, so let's have it for the kids to prevent them from getting in the cycle that they should not be in the first place. So, thank you, Chair. Thank you.
I do have one follow-up question to Council Member Narcisse's line of questioning. Do you have any buildings with green space designed on the top of the building, by chance?

Yeah. Thanks for the question, Chair.

We do. At about 41 or 42 of our Parks facilities, some of which are just sort of, you know, parks, M and O facilities, or what have you, we have several green roofs that absorb, you know, rainwater. You know, broadly speaking, and they also help with, you know, heating costs, cooling costs, things of that nature. Happy to give you a tour of some of our facilities and show some of the great work that's happened.
Okay, I do have some follow-up questions, but I don't want to take up too much time. I'm going to jump to Council Member Morano.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. Thank you both for your testimony, and as a representative of the Borough of Parks, thank you for all the work you're doing for the parks of our city. In your testimony, Deputy Commissioner, you said the mandate to create 300 miles of trails is impractical, and that resources should focus on maintaining existing trails. How many miles of trails today are currently in poor condition, or not

properly maintained, and what would it cost to fix them?

Thank you for that question, Council Member, and the trails in Staten Island are particularly wonderful. We have already formalized 275 miles of trail across the city. As I mentioned in our testimony, we have mapped trails of all sorts of conditions to the extent of about 450 miles, so our process of going through, you know, park by park to really look at what the best and safest network of trails is for every location involves essentially screening out those trails that are not in good condition, that are not safe, that are, you know, perhaps duplicate or redundant, but that don't serve the public, and that's how we essentially got to our goal of formalizing 300 trails. So, we're actually quite aligned. We have a goal of formalizing 300 miles of trails run in our natural areas, and we think we'll be able to achieve that this year. By the end of 2027, or by 2027, we hope to have all those formalized trails actually updated on our Parks website.

You noted that natural areas are most abundant in the Bronx, Queens,

and Staten Island. Of the 300 miles of formalized trails that you say are being delivered, how many miles are actually in Staten Island?
Thank you for the question. It's a great question. I don't actually believe I have that number handy, and we're happy to provide that that after the hearing.

That would be great. Thank you. You rely heavily on the… in discussing Intro. 740, you rely heavily on the Walk to a Park metric, and say that 84.2 percent of New Yorkers have access. Does that metric account for the quality, safety, or usability of those parks, or is it just distance on a map?

Thank you for the question. We fundamentally, Parks, of course, are always concerned about the quality and condition of our parks, so we expect every park to meet a certain standard and work, you know, on a daily basis to achieve that. The metric looks at access to a park that, for the full given hours of a park, you know, period. So, an open space wouldn't be, in a community garden, for example, that's closed

to the public for a given time. So, in general, the conditions of our parks really meet our agency standard when we're accounting for them.

Council Member Wong asked you guys about Intro. 805, and you mentioned a pilot program on cool pavement, and said expansion shouldn't happen just yet. How much has been spent on that pilot so far, and what specific benchmarks need to be met before you move forward or abandon it?

It's a good question. Our understanding from our colleagues at DOT is that they're still in the planning stages. The bill was passed, I believe, late last year, and I believe they're expecting to kick off the pilot, which by law I think was anticipated to last two years, I believe, and I believe they're supposed to kick off in the fall.

And finally, for Intro. 806, the wildlife plan, you already described an existing wildlife unit doing education, monitoring, and management. What specifically would this bill require that isn't already happening today, and what would be the additional cost?

Thanks for the question, Council Member, and I may ask our Chief of Education and Wildlife to correct me if I mischaracterize anything, but what the bill contemplates is the creation of an advisory board of numerous members, including the Parks Department. But because wildlife, you know, our management efforts are pretty strictly focused on property that's under our jurisdiction, you know, 30,000 acres, plenty, and there is certainly a, as you heard, a lot of wildlife, the presence of wildlife is throughout our park system. What the bill seems to contemplate is the creation of an advisory board that takes a citywide sort of perspective and creates a plan. (TIMER CHIME) So, you're asking a very good question about the cost of that. I think it's going to be hard for us to, I'm not sure we're quite aware of that at the moment.
Thank you.
Thank you, Council Member. We're going to jump to Council Member Salaam.

Thank you, Chair, and thank you for your testimony so far.

I want to go into Intro. 805 as well. Community districts with the highest heat vulnerability indices and low median income often have playgrounds and court surfaces that are heavily used year-round by residents who lack access to private recreational spaces or air conditions. Can the Department commit to ensuring that Manhattan pilot sites are located in neighborhood tabulation areas that meet both heat and income thresholds and have the highest recreational surface usage and foot traffic?

Thanks for the question, Council Member. And, as we noted in our testimony, we undergo a lot of interventions to reduce, you know, that sort of heat vulnerability, not the least of which is obviously our planting strategy all over the city, including within parks, but also in our playgrounds, for example, using color treatments, you know, of a lighter color or using safety service of lighter colored tiles. Those are things we very much, you know, are very committed to and advancing. As for the pilot itself, my recollection is that the DOT pilot, which is already, you know, required by law, I believe there is a metric where

they are, I believe, directed to prioritize high heat vulnerability neighborhoods, but I don't want to misspeak so I can double check on that, but my understanding is that's very much part of the guiding principle for that pilot.

Sure. Absolutely. And going into 806, in dense communities where parks are heavily used and bordered by high-density residential buildings, residents face persisting wildlife-related challenges including rat infestations in and around parks. In designated rat mitigation zones, 85 percent of Park property failed initial inspection despite significant investments. Will this wildlife management plan address rat and rodent management alongside charismatic species like coyotes and raptors, and how will the plan prioritize community-level public health concerns?

Yeah. Thanks for the question, Council Member. And I think what I, you know, obviously that the City is, you know, taking rat mitigation efforts very, very seriously. Parks has a dedicated team working closely with Department of Health and the Mayor's Office, and you know, there's been significant funding added, you know, for

targeted teams on the Parks side to help address some of those concerns for sure, and we always want to hear about that and address it as timely as possible. As to whether that aspect would be incorporated, it's hard for us to contemplate what this theoretical advisory board will or won't consider, so you know, respectfully, it's hard, but I don't think we want to speculate whether what they will or won't include.

Well, we definitely want those included, of course. Going into Intro. 740, does DPR currently have internal data on green space per capita at the community district levels? Trust for Public Land data shows that neighborhoods of color have 44 percent less nearby park spaces, and low-income areas have 38 percent less than high-income areas. Can the Department share preliminary findings on which Manhattan community districts fall furthest below the CEQR standard of 2.5 acres per 1,000 residents?

Thank you for the question, Council Member. I don't have that data with us. The community districts that we are focusing on don't

happen to include Manhattan, but we can certainly look at the data that we have for that District and share that with you.

And also, for community districts with higher population density and lower green space per capita, what strategies beyond traditional parkland acquisition has DPR explored? Specifically, has the Department evaluated partnerships with NYCHA to activate the approximately 2,400 acres of NYCHA open space or expansion of Schoolyard to Playground programs which converted 266 schoolyard citywide at 111 million dollars?

I'll just start on the NYCHA front just to, you know, that we've actually worked in close consultation with them on a variety of different efforts, including helping formalize some of their community garden spaces. Now as the Deputy Commissioner noted, that doesn't technically impact our Walk to a Park score, but we still think it's an important, you know, effort that obviously helps beautify and engage, you know, the local residents. And, you know, we've been very, very proud to work with NYCHA on that. And I believe we also have numerous playgrounds

and other areas that are, you know, technically under Parks jurisdiction, but either directly adjacent to or within, you know, NYCHA campuses. So, you know, I'd say we have a very, very close relationship and are always open to exploring, you know, new and additional opportunities. And I'll turn back to the Commissioner on the acquisition piece.

Yes. Thank you for the question. We certainly are very proud of the Schoolyard to Playground Program. We most recently were able to add 11 schoolyards into (TIMER CHIME) that program. And we're, you know, throughout our divisions in the Parks Department, even when, you know, acquisition is difficult, as was mentioned, we work with our community gardens through our Green Thumb Program, and as I previously mentioned, we work with our stewardship program throughout the city to focus on street tree care so we have a lot of emphasis on programming when we have challenges, perhaps, in being able to acquire more open space in dense communities.

Chair, if I may, just one last question? On our Intro. 577, dense inland community districts in Upper Manhattan are adjacent to park properties with significant acreage, steep terrain, and mature tree cover that could support trail infrastructure, yet they currently have no formalized, blazed, or mapped trails. How would DPR ensure that inland districts with high population density and limited existing trail access are prioritized under this bill, rather than concentrating investment in outer borough parks that already have trail networks?

Thank you for that question.
